messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 37
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Psychologist
  trauma_type: Rape
  pcl5: 61

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Locked Spaces: Being in a locked or confined room, Sexual Trauma Cues: Comments on sexual violence, Male Presence: Being alone with men
  Threat: Back to Wall: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room, Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert, Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place
  Negative Appraisals: Hopelessness: I have no future, Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me, Exposed to Others: I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Threat
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Kwame's Story

Kwame was thirty-seven when the attack happened, though he would later mark his life in two distinct eras: before and after a single night in March. He had been at a professional conference in Atlanta, staying in a hotel near the airport, when a man he'd met at the bar—someone who seemed friendly, who had talked about psychology and trauma work—had invited him back to his room. Kwame had gone willingly. He had trusted the conversation, the sense of intellectual kinship. What followed was a violent assault in a locked hotel room, the man's weight pinning him to the bed, his own voice seeming to come from someone else's body as he begged for it to stop. The lock on the door had made escape impossible. The windows looked out onto a parking lot where no one could hear him. When it was over, Kwame had lain there in the dark, feeling the weight of the man's presence even after he'd left the room, and had understood in that moment something that would reshape every day that followed: he was not safe anywhere.

For weeks afterward, Kwame had tried to function. He'd returned to his practice, seeing clients in his office in Durham, a space he'd always found professional and calm. But something had fractured. Within a month, he'd rearranged his entire office so that his desk faced the door and he could see into the waiting room. He'd begun positioning himself with his back against the wall during sessions, a habit so pronounced that one client had asked if he was uncomfortable. He wasn't sleeping well either—his mind wouldn't quiet at night, and he'd lie awake convinced that vigilance was the only thing keeping him alive. The belief that he was fundamentally exposed, that the trauma was written across his face for anyone to read, had begun to calcify. He was certain that his clients could see what had happened to him, that they would sense his weakness, his failure to protect himself. When a female client had mentioned her own experience of assault in passing, Kwame had felt the room tilt. The conversation about sexual violence, innocent as it was, had triggered a cascade of panic—his heart racing, his hands trembling—and he'd had to excuse himself to the bathroom.

The triggers began to multiply in ways that seemed to follow a logic he couldn't quite name. Locked spaces became intolerable. When a client's session ran late and Kwame found himself in his office with the door closed, he would feel his chest tighten, an urgent need to leave that he could barely suppress. But what frightened him most was the presence of men. Being alone with a male colleague, even briefly, sent his nervous system into overdrive. He'd started avoiding meetings that were one-on-one, scheduling consultations only in group settings, making excuses. His supervisor had noticed—had asked if everything was all right—but Kwame couldn't articulate it. How could he explain that the simple fact of a man's presence in an enclosed space had become a threat that his body registered before his mind could reason it away?

What Kwame had come to believe, in the months that followed, was that he had no control over what happened to him, that his future was a foregone conclusion of further harm. He couldn't stop bad things from happening. This conviction didn't sit separately from his vigilance; it fed it. His inability to relax, even in his own apartment with the door locked and the lights on, was rooted in the conviction that relaxation was a luxury he couldn't afford, that the moment he let his guard down was the moment danger would find him. The hypervigilance—the need to position himself so he could see the room, the inability to fall asleep without first checking the locks—became the logical response to a world that had already proven itself catastrophic. And this constant state of threat monitoring, this exhausting surveillance of his environment and of other people's intentions, only deepened his sense of hopelessness. He was trapped in a loop where his fear confirmed his belief that the world was dangerous, and his belief that he was helpless made the fear feel justified.

By the time Kwama called for an appointment, six months had passed. He was thinner, his eyes hollow with sleep deprivation. He'd begun considering whether he could continue practicing as a psychologist—how could he help others when he couldn't help himself? That question, more than any other, had finally pushed him to seek help. He sat in the intake room with his back to the corner, and when asked what had brought him in, he said simply: "I'm drowning, and I don't know how to stop."
